title: Where My Art Is Now
objective: Record a baseline today by making one piece, then writing three words for what it does well and one word for what it does not do yet.

blocks.text: BUILD · Art · Week 1. Trinity Arts Award Bronze. Where My Art Is Now.
Objective: record a baseline today, by making one piece and writing three words for what it does well and one word for what it does not do yet.
Success evidence: one piece made today, four words on the sheet, a ring for each word, and today's date.

Your four words are about the artwork on your desk. You write about marks, colours and shapes. You do not write about your home, your family, your body or what you believe. Nobody in this room is asked about theirs.
Theme: My Creative Identity. Identity here means what your own work keeps choosing.
40 minutes. Offline.

Bronze evidence, read from the register. This deck evidences Bronze Part A, Explore the arts as a participant, which requires active participation in any art form, improvement, and a summary of what they learnt. This lesson is the baseline that the improvement is later measured against. Bronze attempted rule, quoted: "ONE Attempted allowed overall. Any Not Attempted = Below Pass." The evidence file cap is 10 files for the whole Bronze level, so keep this baseline as part of one Part A file rather than starting a new one. The three assessment areas are art form knowledge and understanding, creativity, and communication. Bronze is the Level 1 Award in the Arts. Nothing in this deck is booked and no visit is claimed.

stages.title: Arrival · retrieve
stages.data-ta1: Sheets, pencils and log pages out on desks before pupils sit down. Nobody starts drawing yet.
stages.data-ta2: Say the not yet line out loud once, then write it on the board and leave it there all lesson.

blocks.text: A baseline is where you start
This is week one of your Bronze Arts Award.
A baseline is a record of where you start.
You cannot show you got better with no start.
Bronze Part A asks you to take part in an art form.
It asks you to get better at it.
It asks you to say what you learnt.
Today does the first job of the three.
You make one piece, then you read it.
Then you give the piece four words.
Three words say what the piece does well.
One word says what it does not do yet.
Not yet is the point. It is a job to do, not a fault.
Read the four-word rule once and leave it on the board. Three for what works, one for not yet. Pupils who miss the fourth word have no baseline to improve against.
You need one sheet, one pencil and your log page.

stages.title: Starter · create the need
stages.data-ta1: Hold up both example pieces yourself. Never use a pupil's work as the blank one.

blocks.text: Two pieces, and one of them is a baseline
Look at two pieces by the same maker.
Both were made in week one.
The first piece has no words on it.
The second piece has four words written under it.
Now think about week six.
Only one of them can be used.
The piece with words shows what changed.
The blank piece shows a sheet and nothing more.
Words turn a piece into a baseline.

items: 2 · look at the piece, not at your day.
3 · write three words for what it does well.
4 · write one word for what it does not do yet.

blocks.text: Four words is enough. More words hide the point.

stages.title: I Do · model
stages.data-ta1: Make your own piece in front of them, on a timer. Do not pull a finished exemplar out of a folder.
stages.data-ta2: If a pupil offers a word about their day, their home or their family, say: give me a word for the mark on the paper instead. Then write that word down and move on.

blocks.text: I make one piece and read it
I take one sheet and set a timer.
I draw for six minutes, then I stop.
My piece is small, and that is fine.
A baseline is not your best work.
It is a true record of today.
Now I look at it and say nothing yet.
I put a finger on one part first.
My first word is thick, for the lines at the top.
My second word is grey, for the colour I used.
My third word is curved, for the shapes down the side.
Each word points at a part I can touch.

boxes.head: ONE WORD
boxes.line1: what it does not do yet

blocks.caption: Four steps, and the last one is the word you will work on
blocks.title: The four steps of a baseline
blocks.alt: Four boxes joined by arrows, with a small drawn sheet in the first box and a hand pointing in the second

blocks.text: Now the fourth word, and it works the other way.
It names one thing the piece does not do yet.
My word is flat, because nothing looks near or far.
I write flat in the not yet box.
Then I ring the part each word names.
Draw the rings while they watch, one at a time. A word with no ring is the fault this stage exists to stop.
Watch where my finger goes each time.
A word I cannot point at gets crossed out.

stages.title: We Do · everyone commits
stages.data-ta1: Cards face down until every table is quiet. Then turn them over together.

blocks.text: Sort the word cards, then match them
Six word cards sit on your table.
Each card holds one word from a real baseline.
The cards say thick, rushed, grey, rubbish, curved and smudged.
Sort them into two piles: points at the work, and points at nothing.
A card points at the work if you could touch that part.
Now take the pile that points at the work.
Match each card to what it names.
The three names are a mark, a colour and a shape.
Every card gets a match, even when you are not sure.
A guess I can see beats a blank card.
Then hold up the card your table argued about most.

Adjudication. Points at the work: thick, grey, curved, smudged. Points at nothing: rushed, rubbish. In the match, thick and smudged are marks, grey is a colour, curved is a shape. Smudged is the useful argument, because it is a real mark and it is also a not yet word.

stages.title: I Do 2 · connect
stages.data-ta1: Put both words on the board at once, then invite the group to point at each one on the piece.

blocks.text: A word about the work, not about you
Two words now, on the same piece.
The first word is smudged.
You can find the smudge and point at it.
The second word is rubbish.
You cannot point at rubbish on a page.
Rubbish is about the maker, not the work.

boxes.head: ABOUT THE WORK
boxes.line2: your finger lands on a part

blocks.caption: Same piece, and only one kind of word can be checked
blocks.title: Words that land against words that do not
blocks.alt: Two boxes side by side, one with a hand touching a marked sheet and one with a hand held over a blank space

blocks.text: There is a quick test for any word.
Ask if two people would pick the same part.
Two people can both find the thick lines.
Two people cannot both find rubbish.
Your not yet word takes the same test.
Flat, empty and faint all pass it.
Lazy and bad do not, so leave them out.
This is why the words stay on the artwork.

items: 2 · put a finger on the part it names.
3 · keep the word if your finger landed.
4 · swap the word if it did not.

stages.title: We Do 2 · lab
stages.data-ta1: Pair by table, not by choice. Call time out loud at two minutes each way.
stages.data-ta2: A pupil who will not swap sheets tests their own four words with an adult instead, out loud.

blocks.text: Test a partner's four words
Work in twos and swap sheets.
Read your partner's first word out loud.
Then try to point at the part it names.
If your finger lands, tick the word.
If it does not, write a cross by it.
A cross means swap the word, not rub it out.
Do all four words, then swap back.
You are testing the words, not the art.
Never tell a partner their piece is good or bad.
Tell them which word your finger found.

stages.title: Independent · evidence
stages.data-ta1: Scribe the pupil's exact word. Do not upgrade a short word into a better one.
stages.data-ta2: A pupil who cannot write may point at a part and say the word. The adult writes it and rings that part.

blocks.text: Your piece, your four words
Work on your own now.
Make one piece in the time given.
Stop when the timer goes, finished or not.
A stopped piece is still a baseline.
Now write three words for what it does well.
Then write one word for what it does not do yet.
Ring the part of the piece each word names.
Four words, four rings.
Write today's date under the last word.
This sheet is your baseline for Part A.

items: Supported · make the piece and write two words, with a ring for each one.
Standard · make the piece, write three words and one not yet word, and ring the part each word names.
Stretch · as Standard, and write one line saying which word you want to change first.

blocks.text: If you finish early, write what you would try next time.

stages.title: Exit · Audience and Influence
stages.data-ta1: The named adult reads the four words back word for word, then points at one ring. No praise, no paraphrase.

blocks.text: Say your four words to an adult
Read your four words to the adult at your table.
They read them back to you word for word.
Then they point at one ring on your sheet.
If they cannot find it, move the ring.
That adult is your audience today.
Your words changed where they looked.
Now pick one thing that happens next. Keep the not yet word, swap it, or make the same piece again.
Write your pick on the sheet with today's date.
Your sheet goes in the arts log folder, not in your bag.
